answer: Sensitivity analysis tests how robust a cost-effectiveness conclusion is to uncertainty in its inputs. One-way analysis varies one parameter at a time to identify the most influential drivers, often displayed in a tornado diagram that ranks parameters by their effect on the result. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) goes further by varying all uncertain parameters simultaneously, drawing each from a probability distribution to generate thousands of possible outcomes. Together these methods reveal whether a base-case finding that a program is cost-effective holds up once the uncertainty in every estimate is acknowledged.

faqs.q: What is the difference between one-way and probabilistic sensitivity analysis?
faqs.a: One-way sensitivity analysis varies a single parameter at a time to find influential inputs, while probabilistic sensitivity analysis varies all uncertain parameters together by sampling from their distributions to produce a full range of outcomes.

faqs.q: What does a tornado diagram show in a cost-effectiveness analysis?
faqs.a: A tornado diagram ranks parameters by how much each one moves the cost-effectiveness result when varied across its plausible range, with the widest bars at the top identifying the most influential inputs.

faqs.q: Why run probabilistic sensitivity analysis if the base case already looks cost-effective?
faqs.a: Every input in the base case is an estimate. PSA samples thousands of parameter combinations to show the probability that the program remains cost-effective, exposing conclusions that depend on favorable assumptions.
